<reason>Side B (PRO) wins on the decisive antitrust stability argument and the athlete welfare framing. Once schools directly share revenue, B correctly argues that antitrust law prohibits unilateral compensation caps, and only the non-statutory labor exemption provided by collective bargaining offers durable legal immunity. A's alternatives—wishing for a congressional exemption or relying on the House settlement—are legally fragile (settlements don't bind future recruits) or speculative. B also wins the moral clash by reframing A's opposition to workers' compensation and arbitration as a desire to deny injured athletes basic protections while universities profit from their labor. A's tax and Title IX concerns are plausible but effectively countered by B's graduate student analogy and democratic voting argument. B's case provides a cleaner, more legally grounded path to victory on the proposition as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 7), where B answers the pressure questions on antitrust immunity and Olympic sports funding, then delivers the devastating pivot: "Picture a lineman who tears his knee generating millions in television revenue. The opposition wants universities to deny him workers' compensation and let coaches cut him without neutral review." This reframes A's entire "employment cascade" argument as a defense of management prerogative over athlete welfare, neutralizing A's tax and Title IX points by subordinating them to the moral imperative of basic workplace protections.</best_rebuttal>
